title: Divorce and Blended Families: A Bible Study for Starting Over
subtitle: A five-session study on grief, Scripture, children, stepfamilies, and the church, for people walking through divorce, the remarried, and the families and churches that love them.
summary:
This study is for people whose marriages have ended or are ending, for the remarried, for stepparents and stepchildren of any age, and for the churches that love them, or ought to. Its five sessions take up the grief and shame of a marriage's end, read alongside Malachi 2 and Psalm 34; what Jesus and Paul taught about divorce and remarriage, with the three main Christian views stated as their own defenders would; the children caught in the middle; the slow work of a blended family, read through Ruth and Naomi; and the church as family for people whose families have broken. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation, and each ends in prayer rather than advice.

Safety comes first throughout. Scripture never requires anyone to stay in danger, and no one should be counseled to return to it; the leader's primer says what to do if someone discloses abuse, danger, or thoughts of suicide. This guide is not legal advice or counseling. Divorce, custody, and support law vary by state, and the study points people to lawyers, advocates, and licensed counselors for what a small group can't give.

The study refuses the two answers churches have often given divorced people: a verdict, with a verse quoted in the lobby and a quiet removal from the places they served, and a silence, with friends who disappear and ministries built as though every family were intact. Each alone tells a divorced person there is no place for them anymore. The study holds the lifelong intent of marriage and the dignity of divorced people together, leaves open what faithful churches answer differently, and implicates the writer and the leader with everyone else. Most of us have broken faith in smaller ways, and many of us have been the friend who went quiet.
audience: People walking through divorce, remarried couples, stepparents and stepchildren, and the churches that love them

sessions.title: Near to the Brokenhearted
sessions.aim: To name the grief and shame of a marriage's ending without hurrying past either, to read Malachi 2:13-16 in its setting and in the Berean Standard Bible's wording, and to hear that the God who hates the breaking of faith is near to the people it broke, including those grieving their own part in it.
sessions.summary:
A marriage can end in one conversation or over ten years, and it takes more than a spouse: a home, a routine, friends you knew as a couple, holidays, sometimes daily time with your children, and the future you had planned. Some people are ashamed of what was done to them, some of what they did, and many of both. This session doesn't ask anyone to explain their divorce. It asks what God says to people whose marriages have ended, beginning with a verse many of them have had quoted at them.

Malachi told men weeping at the altar that God no longer accepted their offerings because "the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith" (Malachi 2:14). The Berean Standard Bible makes God the one who hates divorce in the verse that follows: "For I hate divorce" (Malachi 2:16). Translations differ there, but on every reading the anger falls on the one who broke faith, and the passage stands with the wife who was sent away. The same Scriptures say, "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit" (Psalm 34:18). Divorce is a real loss and often a real wrong. It is not anyone's name.

keyScripture.why: The prophet tells men weeping at the altar that God no longer receives their offerings because "the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith" (Malachi 2:14). The verse so often quoted at divorced people, "For I hate divorce" (Malachi 2:16), stands in a passage whose sympathy is with the wife who was sent away.

discussion.q: When your marriage ended, or when you watched someone else's end, what was lost besides the person? Name one loss nobody seemed to notice.
discussion.behind: Start with the losses, not the reasons; few people have ever been asked about the in-laws, the couple friends, or the holidays. Don't let anyone explain why their marriage ended, because this session doesn't need the story. Anyone may pass. If the room is slow, go first.

discussion.q: Read Malachi 2:13-16 aloud. Who is weeping at the altar, why does God refuse their offerings, and whose side is the prophet on?
discussion.behind: Let the room find the setting before anyone applies the verse. Malachi speaks to men who broke faith with the wives of their youth and then wept because God refused their worship; the violence in verse 16 is what the husband did. Some here have had this passage used against them. Let them notice whom it was spoken against.

discussion.q: The Berean Standard Bible makes God the one who hates, "For I hate divorce" (Malachi 2:16), while some other translations read the verse as describing a husband who hates his wife and divorces her. Either way, what does God hate here, and what doesn't the passage say?
discussion.behind: Be accurate: translations differ because the Hebrew is difficult, not because anyone is softening it. On any reading the anger falls on the breaking of faith and the harm it does, and nothing says God hates divorced people or is finished with anyone. Let people say what they were told the verse meant.

discussion.q: Psalm 31, which bears David's name, says of the one praying, "they flee when they see me on the street" (Psalm 31:11). Where have you felt avoided, or where have you avoided someone whose marriage ended, and why?
discussion.behind: This is the turn toward self-implication. Shame after divorce is social as much as moral, and many of us have been the friend who went quiet, a quiet that felt like a verdict. Let both kinds of answers come. If you can truthfully name a time you went quiet, say it first.

discussion.q: "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit" (Psalm 34:18). What would it mean for you to believe God is near, not only to what was done to you, but to what you did?
discussion.behind: Some in the room were wronged, some did wrong, and many are both, which is why the verse names the brokenhearted and the contrite together. Don't press anyone to sort out fault tonight. God's nearness doesn't wait for the sorting to be finished; leave the question open.

objections.objection: God hates divorce. That's in the Bible. If churches stop saying so, there will be more of it, and the church will lose one of the few things it still says clearly about marriage.
objections.response: Grant what is true in it. Scripture takes marriage seriously, Jesus called it a joining God makes (Matthew 19:6), and a church that shrugs at broken vows teaches its children that promises don't matter. The Berean Standard Bible does make God the one who hates divorce, "For I hate divorce" (Malachi 2:16), and no honest reading softens the anger in that passage. But look at whom the anger falls on: husbands who had broken faith with the wives of their youth (Malachi 2:14). Quoting the verse at a woman who was abandoned, or at a man whose wife walked out, turns the passage upside down. A church can teach that marriage is meant to last a lifetime and still meet every divorced person as someone grieving a real loss. Malachi aimed that word at the one who broke faith, not at the one who was broken.

objections.objection: All this talk about grief and shame lets people off the hook. Most divorces involve sin, and if nobody says so, nobody repents.
objections.response: Grant it; grief that never gets around to confession can harden into self-pity. Psalm 31 holds both in one breath: "For my life is consumed with grief and my years with groaning; my iniquity has drained my strength" (Psalm 31:10). But timing is part of truthfulness. Someone in the first weeks of a divorce will often hear a call to repentance as a verdict on their worth. Stay long enough to say both things, each to the right person; many in this room were the ones sinned against. Where someone did wrong, the promise is plain: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you could tell God one true sentence tonight about how you are really doing, without explaining or defending yourself, what would it be?
sessions.practice: This week, list what you lost when your marriage ended, one line for each loss: the house, the in-laws, the friends, the future you pictured. Then pray through the list with Psalm 31. Where you were wronged, say so to God; where you did wrong, say that too. Tell one person how you are really doing. If you are afraid of your spouse or former spouse, start with safety instead: call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788, and call 911 in immediate danger. If your marriage isn't over, the care page at /help/marriage may serve you better.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you were a witness when our vows were made, and you have seen everything since. You know what was done to us and what we have done. Some of us are angry tonight, some ashamed, and most of us are tired. You hate the breaking of faith, and you are near to the brokenhearted, and we need both to be true. Forgive us where we broke faith, and where we were broken, bind up the wound. Forgive your church its verdicts and its silences, and us our share in both. Keep anyone in danger safe, and guard every child caught between two houses. In the name of Jesus, who was despised and rejected and knew our grief. Amen.
reflection: What did I lose when this marriage ended, and which of those losses have I never grieved?
Where have I heard Malachi 2:16 used, and what changes when I read it in its setting?
Where am I among the brokenhearted, where among the contrite, and do I believe God is near to both?
sessions.teaching:
A divorce is a death in which no one dies. The person you married is still alive, still sending messages about school pickups, perhaps sitting in the bleachers at your son's game, and there is no funeral, no meal brought to the door, and no one sure whether they're allowed to mention it. What ended was a whole household: its routines and holidays, the in-laws who had become family, the friends you knew as a couple, the future you were planning. All of it goes at once.

Shame usually comes with the grief. Some people are ashamed of what was done to them, being left or betrayed; others of what they did, the affair, the years of coldness, the leaving. Many carry both, and almost no one carries it out loud. Shame is part of why some divorced people slip out before the last song on Sunday. Psalm 31, which bears David's name, describes it from the inside: "they flee when they see me on the street" (Psalm 31:11), and "I am like a broken vessel" (Psalm 31:12).

Churches have often made this harder in two opposite ways. Some handed down a verdict, treating every divorced person as the guilty party, quietly moving them out of the places they served, and quoting a verse from Malachi as though it settled everything. Others said nothing and called the silence grace. The verdict remembers that Scripture takes marriage seriously; the silence remembers that a wounded person needs presence before instruction. But each one, alone, tells a divorced person that there is no longer a place for them here. Those of us who lead churches are inside that failure, and so is anyone leading this study.

So begin with the verse. Malachi preached to Judah in the Persian period, after the exile, most likely in the middle of the fifth century BC. Men married women who worshiped other gods (Malachi 2:11), and some were sending away the wives they had married when they were young, perhaps to marry into wealthier families. Then they wept at the altar and couldn't understand why God refused their offerings. Malachi tells them: "It is because the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant" (Malachi 2:14).

The next verse is among the hardest Hebrew in the prophets, and translations differ. The Berean Standard Bible, like the King James, makes God the one who hates divorce: "For I hate divorce" (Malachi 2:16). The NIV of 2011, the CSB, and the ESV read it instead as describing the husband who hates, or does not love, his wife and divorces her. On any reading the anger falls on the one who breaks faith, and the violence the verse names is what he did to her: "He who divorces his wife covers his garment with violence" (Malachi 2:16). Jewish tradition grieved over such divorces: the Babylonian Talmud closes its tractate on divorce with a rabbi's saying that even the altar weeps over a man who divorces the wife of his youth. Read in its setting, the verse indicts the one who broke faith and passes no sentence on the one he left.

The same Scriptures give some of God's tenderest words to the one who was sent away. In Isaiah, God speaks to his exiled people as a discarded wife and calls her home: "For the LORD has called you back, like a wife deserted and wounded in spirit, like the rejected wife of one's youth" (Isaiah 54:6). The people had been sent away for their own transgressions (Isaiah 50:1), and still God promised, "with great compassion I will bring you back" (Isaiah 54:7). His tenderness reaches the one who was betrayed and the one who did the betraying.

Psalm 34 also bears David's name, and its heading sets it on the day a king drove him away. At its center stands this line: "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit" (Psalm 34:18). The brokenhearted are the ones something was done to. The contrite are the ones who know they did something. In many divorces they are the same person at different hours of the same day, and God is near to both before the sorting is finished.

So the first word to a divorced person is the truth, told in the right order. Divorce is a real loss and often a real wrong, sometimes on both sides, sometimes mostly on one. Where you were wronged, you may grieve it as a wrong, and God takes your side as Malachi did. Where you did wrong, you can name it and be forgiven (1 John 1:9). Shame says you are ruined. The gospel says you are known. And if the person you married frightens you, safety comes before every other conversation, including any talk of reconciliation.

scriptureStudy.note: "It is because the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith" (Malachi 2:14). The tears at the altar are the husbands'. God refuses their worship because of what they did to their wives, and he was witness to the vows they broke.

The Berean Standard Bible renders the hard Hebrew of verse 16 as God's own hatred of divorce; several recent translations read it as describing the husband who hates his wife and divorces her. Either way, "He who divorces his wife covers his garment with violence" (Malachi 2:16), and the anger lands on the one who breaks faith.

"Do not be afraid, for you will not be put to shame" (Isaiah 54:4). God speaks to his exiled people as a wife sent away, though they had been sent away for their own transgressions (Isaiah 50:1), and promises "with great compassion I will bring you back" (Isaiah 54:7).
"For my life is consumed with grief and my years with groaning; my iniquity has drained my strength" (Psalm 31:10). This psalm holds grief, guilt, and the shame of being avoided in a single prayer.

"The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit" (Psalm 34:18). The heading sets the psalm on the day a king drove David away. Nearness is promised to the wounded and to the sorry alike.

"If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). Where someone did wrong in a marriage, the way out is neither hiding it nor defending it, but naming it to a God who is faithful to forgive.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long history behind the verse. The law of Moses didn't invent divorce; it regulated a practice already present, requiring a husband who sent his wife away to give her a certificate proving she was free to marry again (Deuteronomy 24:1-4). By the first century teachers argued over how easily a man could do it, and the Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, records the schools of Shammai and Hillel on opposite sides (Gittin 9:10). The same tradition that regulated divorce grieved it, as the saying about the altar's tears shows.

Weigh, too, the difference between guilt and shame. Guilt says I did something wrong, and Scripture answers it with confession and forgiveness (Psalm 32:5; 1 John 1:9). Shame says I am something wrong, and Scripture answers it with covering and restoration, as when God clothed the man and woman before they left the garden (Genesis 3:21), or told his exiled people, "Do not be afraid, for you will not be put to shame" (Isaiah 54:4). A church that offers only the first will leave people forgiven and still hiding. The life page at /life/shame-and-the-hiding-self takes the distinction further.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose that in the first session a woman mentions, almost in passing, that she stopped going to her old church after her husband left, because a man there told her that God hates divorce. Across the circle, a man who left his own marriage three years ago goes very still. Someone else says her old church was right about the verse, if wrong to say it to her.

Don't rush to settle who was right about Malachi. Thank each of them, read Malachi 2:14 and 2:16 aloud, and ask to whom the prophet was speaking. Let the group discover that the verse she was handed comes from a passage that takes her side. Then read Psalm 34:18 and let the man hear it too. Afterward, speak privately with each of them, and if the woman is afraid of her former husband, help her reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline.

Use this to show the room that one passage can shield the betrayed and call the one who broke faith to repentance, and that a church needs to know which word it is speaking, and to whom.

sessions.title: What God Has Joined
sessions.aim: To read Jesus' teaching in Matthew 19:3-9 and Paul's in 1 Corinthians 7:10-16 in their settings, to state the three main Christian positions on divorce and remarriage in the form their own defenders would sign, and to hold the floor beneath all of them: no reading of Scripture requires anyone to stay in danger.
sessions.summary:
Ask a room of Christians what the Bible says about divorce and remarriage and you will hear confident answers that don't agree, each often taught as the only Christian view.

When Pharisees asked Jesus, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?" (Matthew 19:3), they wanted him to take a side in a dispute over Deuteronomy 24. He went back to creation instead: "So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate" (Matthew 19:6). He called Moses' permission a concession to hardness of heart, and in Matthew he names one exception. Paul passed on the Lord's command and then took up a case Jesus hadn't addressed, a believer whose unbelieving spouse leaves: "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace" (1 Corinthians 7:15).

Faithful churches read these words differently, and this session lets each view speak at its strongest without choosing among them. What it says plainly is the floor beneath all three: Scripture never requires anyone to stay in danger, and abuse is a breaking of the marriage covenant by the abuser, not by the one who flees. The views part over what follows for remarriage; none of them sends a frightened spouse home.

keyScripture.why: Asked whether a man may divorce his wife "for any reason" (Matthew 19:3), Jesus answers from creation, calls Moses' certificate a concession to hardness of heart, and names an exception that Christians have read in different ways ever since. Any Christian view of divorce and remarriage has to account for the whole of it.

discussion.q: What were you taught about divorce and remarriage, and by whom? Did anyone ever tell you that faithful Christians disagree about it?
discussion.behind: Surface the inherited answers before reading anything, and don't correct anyone yet. Many will be surprised that churches confessing the same creeds read these passages differently. If someone was hurt by one of these answers, let them say so without debate.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 19:3-9. The Pharisees asked about divorce "for any reason" (Matthew 19:3). Where does Jesus start his answer, and why does it matter that he starts there?
discussion.behind: Jesus refuses to begin with grounds. He begins with what marriage is, two made one flesh by God (Genesis 2:24). Point out the setting in the teaching notes: two schools argued over Deuteronomy 24:1, and only a husband could send a wife away. Jesus' words bound the one who held the power.

discussion.q: Mark and Luke record Jesus' saying without the exception Matthew includes (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18), and Mark says the man who divorces his wife and remarries "commits adultery against her" (Mark 10:11). What do you notice when you read the accounts side by side?
discussion.behind: This is where the views part, so read slowly and don't hurry to resolve it. Some take the shorter sayings as the rule and read Matthew's exception narrowly; others take the exception as part of what Jesus taught everywhere. Point out what only Mark records: the wife sent away is the one wronged.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 7:10-16. Paul says, "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases" (1 Corinthians 7:15). What might "not bound" mean here, and what is true for the one who was left on any reading?
discussion.behind: Christians read the phrase not bound in two main ways: free to remarry, or free from the duty to hold the marriage together. Let both be heard. Then name what every reading shares: the one who was left didn't do the leaving, and "God has called you to live in peace" (1 Corinthians 7:15). The one who was left may need that sentence most.

discussion.q: This study states three Christian positions on remarriage and doesn't choose among them. Which is hardest for you to hear in its strongest form, and what does that view protect that you would not want the church to lose?
discussion.behind: This is the self-implication. Each view guards something good: the faithfulness of a vow, the freedom of the betrayed and the abandoned, and a future for someone whose spouse made the marriage a danger. Ask each person, you first, to name what the view they find hardest gets right. Don't let the room vote, and keep the floor in view: no view requires anyone to stay in danger.

objections.objection: Jesus said that what God has joined, no one should separate. If the church allows remarriage after divorce, it is just giving people what they want and calling it grace.
objections.response: Grant its strength: it takes Jesus' hardest words at face value. Mark and Luke record the saying with no exception (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18), Paul writes, "A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives" (1 Corinthians 7:39), and the early church largely held that view, as many faithful Christians do today. But the other views are not simply concessions to desire. Matthew records Jesus' own exception (Matthew 19:9), Paul says the deserted believer is "not bound in such cases" (1 Corinthians 7:15), and God himself says of faithless Israel, "I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away" (Jeremiah 3:8). Christians who permit remarriage on those grounds are trying to obey the same Lord from the same texts. Hold your conviction, and grant that a brother or sister who reads it differently may be just as serious about Jesus as you are.

objections.objection: My husband beat me. I don't care what any view says about remarriage. I'm not going back, and nobody should tell me I have to.
objections.response: You are right, and no faithful reading of Scripture says otherwise. Abuse breaks the marriage covenant, and the one who breaks it is the abuser, not the one who flees. Even Christians who hold that remarriage is not permitted while a former spouse lives teach that separation can be right, and Paul's instructions already make room for a wife who has separated (1 Corinthians 7:11). No church should send a frightened spouse home. In immediate danger, call 911; the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788, can help you plan, which matters because leaving can be the most dangerous time. What faithful churches differ on is what follows for remarriage, and that question can wait until you are safe.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you could ask Jesus one question about your own marriage, or someone else's, what would it be, and what do you hope he would say?
sessions.practice: This week, read Matthew 19:3-12, Mark 10:2-12, and 1 Corinthians 7:1-17 in one sitting and write down every question you have. Then write the strongest case you can for the view of remarriage you find hardest to accept. If you are deciding something about your own marriage, take your questions to a pastor who will hear your whole story; if there has been violence or fear, start with safety and call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. If the session stirred guilt over your own part in a marriage's end, pray Psalm 51.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, when they asked you about grounds, you went back to the beginning and told us what marriage is before you told us what it isn't. We confess that we have used your words as weapons and as loopholes, binding burdens on people we never helped and treating vows as though they cost nothing. Give us humility where faithful people disagree and honesty where we have sinned. Protect everyone in danger tonight. Where we were left, give us peace. Where we did the leaving, give us truth. You were faithful to us when we were not. Make us faithful now. Amen.
reflection: Which view of divorce and remarriage did I inherit, and have I ever heard the others in their strongest form?
What does each view protect that I would not want the church to lose?
If I am facing a decision about my own marriage, who will hear my whole story and help me read Scripture honestly?
sessions.teaching:
Most people come to this session with a verdict in hand, and few were told that churches confessing the same creeds have read these passages differently for centuries. This session reads the passages behind the verdicts, states each view as its own defenders would, and names the floor none of them may move.

Start where Jesus' questioners started. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 assumed that a man might send his wife away and required him to give her a certificate, which protected her freedom to marry again. By the first century, teachers argued over the grounds it allowed: the Mishnah records that the school of Shammai permitted divorce only for unchastity, the school of Hillel even if a wife spoiled her husband's dinner. Only the husband could issue a divorce. So when Pharisees asked whether a man could divorce his wife "for any reason" (Matthew 19:3), they were asking Jesus to choose a side.

Jesus refused to start there. He went back to creation: "So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate" (Matthew 19:6). Pressed about Moses, he said, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart; but it was not this way from the beginning" (Matthew 19:8). Then: "Now I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman, commits adultery" (Matthew 19:9). Whatever else is disputed, he refused to treat marriage as disposable.

Mark and Luke give the saying without the exception (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18), and Mark's account says that the man who divorces and remarries "commits adultery against her" (Mark 10:11): under Jewish law, where only the husband could send the wife away, Jesus named the wife as the one wronged. Paul, writing around AD 53 to 55, passed on the Lord's command: "A wife must not separate from her husband. But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband" (1 Corinthians 7:10-11). Then he took up a believer whose unbelieving spouse leaves: "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace" (1 Corinthians 7:15). In Roman law, leaving a marriage with intent to end it was itself a divorce, so Paul's words for separating and divorcing overlap.

From these texts faithful Christians have reached three main positions. The first holds that marriage binds until death, so that remarriage while a former spouse lives is not permitted. Its defenders point to the sayings in Mark and Luke, to Paul's "A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives" (1 Corinthians 7:39), and to the early church, which largely held this view; the Catholic Church teaches a form of it. They read Matthew's exception as allowing separation only, or narrowly, as unfaithfulness during betrothal (Matthew 1:19) or a marriage the law forbade. This view's comfort is a vow kept the way God keeps his, as Hosea was told to love his unfaithful wife again (Hosea 3:1), and a door left open to reconciliation.

The second holds that sexual unfaithfulness and desertion free the wronged spouse to divorce and remarry. Its defenders read Jesus' exception (Matthew 19:9; 5:32) as permitting divorce and remarriage after adultery, and Paul's "not bound" (1 Corinthians 7:15) as the same freedom after desertion, and they note that God himself says of faithless Israel, "I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away" (Jeremiah 3:8). Many Protestant churches have held it since the Reformation, and the Westminster Confession of 1646 teaches it. Its comfort is that the betrayed and the abandoned are not made to carry the betrayer's sin for life.

The third, a wider view, counts abuse and other grave breaking of the vows as desertion or as breaking the covenant itself. It points to the law's protection of a neglected wife, who "is free to go without monetary payment" (Exodus 21:11), and to Paul's call to peace; many Protestant churches now hold some form of it. Its comfort is that no one is bound to a covenant the other turned into a danger. Beside all three, the Orthodox churches, by a pastoral mercy called economia, allow a second marriage with prayers of repentance.

Here the study stops, deliberately. This question divides faithful churches, not the faith; the creeds don't settle it. What the views share is larger than where they part: marriage is meant to last a lifetime, breaking faith is a real wrong, and no divorce is beyond forgiveness for anyone who confesses. And all of them stand on a floor this study will not move. Scripture never requires anyone to stay in danger. Abuse is a breaking of the marriage covenant, and the one who breaks it is the abuser, not the spouse who flees. Where the views differ is whether that breaking frees the wronged spouse to remarry. Even those who hold that remarriage is not permitted teach that separation can be right (1 Corinthians 7:11), and no church should send a frightened spouse home.

Each tradition also has a besetting sin. Churches that hold the strictest view have sometimes bound heavy burdens on the betrayed and the abused; churches that hold the widest have sometimes made vows cheap and blessed every exit. Both grow from the same root, the wish for a rule that spares us from knowing the actual person. Jesus answered a question about grounds by talking about what God joins. A church that honors him will begin where he began, keep the floor of safety firm, and know a person's story before it speaks about their future.

scriptureStudy.note: "He may write her a certificate of divorce, hand it to her, and send her away from his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1). The law assumed that divorce happened and regulated it. The certificate protected a woman who was sent away by proving she was free to marry again.

"Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart; but it was not this way from the beginning" (Matthew 19:8). The concession is real, and so is the exception that follows (Matthew 19:9), which Christians have read in several ways.

"Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her" (Mark 10:11). Mark and Luke give the saying without the exception, and Mark names the wife as the one wronged, where Jewish law let only the husband issue a divorce.

"The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases" (1 Corinthians 7:15). The phrase not bound is read as freedom to remarry or as freedom from the duty to hold the marriage together. On either reading, the one who was left did not do the leaving.

"I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away" (Jeremiah 3:8). God uses the language of divorce for his judgment on faithless Israel, and in the same chapter pleads, "Return, O faithless Israel" (Jeremiah 3:12). Both those who permit divorce after adultery and those who stress reconciliation read this chapter closely.

"If, however, he does not provide her with these three things, she is free to go without monetary payment" (Exodus 21:11). The law protected even a slave wife from neglect. Christians who hold the wider view read this as evidence that Scripture recognized more than one way a marriage covenant could be broken.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the history of these readings, because the debate is centuries old. The early church largely held that a divorced believer should not remarry while a former spouse lived. The medieval Western church came to treat marriage as a sacrament, and the Council of Trent, at its twenty-fourth session in 1563, defended the indissolubility of a valid marriage against the Reformers. Erasmus had argued in 1519 that the innocent party could remarry, many Protestant churches followed some form of that reading, and the Westminster Confession of 1646 allowed divorce and remarriage for adultery and for desertion that neither church nor magistrate could remedy. The Orthodox took another path, holding marriage to be lifelong in intent while allowing a second marriage, with a penitential rite, as an act of pastoral mercy.

Then weigh the modern books listed at the back: one defending the early church's refusal of remarriage, one reading Jesus against first-century Jewish divorce law, and two multi-view books in which each defender answers the others. Practice stating each position so well that its holders would recognize themselves; that is worth more than a verdict.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a couple in your group were both divorced before they met. In the second session the husband says quietly that a former pastor told them their marriage is adultery, and they have wondered ever since whether God accepts them. A woman whose husband left her for someone else says she believes she is still married in God's eyes and will not remarry.

Resist the pull to rule on either story. Thank them all, and ask the group to state each of the three views in its strongest form, including the one they hold least. Let the room notice that the couple and the woman are both trying to obey the same Lord, and make sure everyone hears what the views share: no divorce is beyond forgiveness, and no one is required to stay in danger. Afterward, speak privately with the couple and with the woman, and encourage each to take their questions to a pastor who will hear the whole story.

Use this to show the room that a second-order question can be held with conviction and charity at once. Ask which view they have been quickest to dismiss.

memoryVerse.text: But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace.

sessions.title: Caught in the Middle
sessions.aim: To see children of divorce, young and grown, as people with their own grief and their own standing before God; to hear Ephesians 6:4 as a limit on parental power that forbids making children messengers, spies, confidants, or judges; and to tell the difference between co-parenting with someone difficult and co-parenting with someone unsafe.
sessions.summary:
The adults chose the divorce, or one of them did. The children chose none of it and live inside all of it: two houses, two sets of rules, holidays cut in half. Many quietly believe the divorce was their fault, or that they could fix it. Many are drawn, usually without anyone meaning to, into the adults' conflict, carrying messages, reporting on the other house, comforting a parent who cries, or being asked to choose.

The letter to the Ephesians speaks to the parent who holds the power: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). The same passage tells children to honor their father and mother, both of them, which is part of why making a child take sides asks the child to carry what God never placed on them. Co-parenting with an ex who is merely difficult calls for patience, brief messages, and freedom for the children to love both parents. Co-parenting with an ex who is unsafe calls for protection, a lawyer, and an advocate, and never for a child left to manage an adult's danger. Through Ezekiel, God refused a proverb that said the children are punished for their fathers' sins (Ezekiel 18:2-4). The consequences of a divorce reach the children. The guilt does not.

keyScripture.why: The household instructions tell children to honor their father and mother and then limit the power of the one who held it: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath" (Ephesians 6:4). After a divorce the children still have two parents, and each holds a power that can form a child or embitter one.

discussion.q: If your parents divorced, at any age, what did you need from the adults around you that you didn't get? If you are a parent, what do you most fear your children are carrying?
discussion.behind: Many adults in the room were once children of divorce, and some have never said so in church. Don't let anyone argue with a childhood memory, and receive a parent's fear or guilt without fixing it. Anyone may pass. If someone describes being harmed as a child, thank them and talk privately afterward.

discussion.q: Read Ephesians 6:1-4. What happens to a child who is told to honor both parents while one parent is asking them to take sides?
discussion.behind: The commandment names both parents, and a divorce doesn't erase either. A child recruited against one parent carries a loyalty conflict God never assigned. Be careful about an unsafe parent: honor never means submitting to abuse, and protecting a child from danger is not teaching dishonor.

discussion.q: Name the roles children get pushed into during a divorce: messenger, spy, confidant, judge, prize. Which have you seen, or slipped into yourself, and why do adults slip into them so easily?
discussion.behind: This is the self-implication. Most parents who use a child this way don't set out to; they are exhausted, lonely, or afraid, and the child is there. Make the roles concrete, from messages about money to being asked where they want to live. Let the room confess before it accuses anyone.

discussion.q: Read 1 Kings 3:16-28. The woman who loved the child would rather lose her claim than see him cut in two. What would it look like in a divorce to refuse to let the children be divided in order to win?
discussion.behind: Be clear that the story shows Solomon's wisdom and is not a rule for custody. Its point is a love that put the child's life ahead of winning. Where the other parent is dangerous, the same love fights to protect the child, through a lawyer and an advocate.

discussion.q: Paul writes, "If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone" (Romans 12:18). What is the difference between an ex who is difficult and one who is unsafe, and what does "on your part" mean in each case?
discussion.behind: Draw the line plainly. A difficult ex is late, rude, or inconsistent; the answer is brief written messages, a shared calendar, and keeping the conflict away from the children. An unsafe ex hits, threatens, stalks, controls, or endangers the children; the answer is a lawyer, an advocate, and the protections a court can give. Nothing here is legal advice.

objections.objection: Children are resilient. They bounce back. Talking this much about the children just piles guilt on parents who are already drowning.
objections.response: Grant what is true. Many children of divorce grow into steady, loving adults, and a parent drowning in guilt is not much use to a child. Guilt is not the aim here. But resilience is not something children manufacture alone. It grows when adults keep them out of the middle, tell them the truth in words that fit their age, let them love both parents where both are safe, and keep their routines steady. When the disciples kept children away from Jesus, "He was indignant" (Mark 10:14). A church that follows him won't leave children to bounce back alone, and it will help their parents carry what is too heavy for one adult.

objections.objection: My ex is a liar and a bad influence. If I don't tell my kids the truth about their other parent, who will?
objections.response: Take the hurt seriously; it may be justified, and children do need the truth in time. But telling a child the truth is different from recruiting a child against their parent. Running down the other parent where the children can hear asks them to carry an adult's anger. Tell them what their safety and their age require, and take the rest to a counselor, a friend, or your prayers; the psalms are full of anger spoken to God rather than to children. Where the other parent is not safe, protect the children through a lawyer, an advocate, and the court, and tell them plainly that keeping them safe is your job, not theirs. "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath" (Ephesians 6:4) applies to the parent with the better case too.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the children in your life could tell you one thing they need from you right now, without any fear of hurting you, what do you think it would be?
sessions.practice: This week, if you are a parent, notice one way your children are standing in the middle, stop it, and take that adult conversation to an adult. Tell each child, in words that fit their age, that the divorce is not their fault and not theirs to fix, and that they may love their other parent if that parent is safe. If the other parent is not safe, talk with your lawyer and an advocate, not with the children, and if a child tells you someone is hurting them, call the police or your state's child protective services. If you are a grown child of divorce, name one message you have been carrying between your parents and set it down. The care page at /help/parenting has more for worn-out parents.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father of the fatherless, you hear the voices of children when the adults around them are too busy fighting to listen. Forgive us for the times we have made our children carry what was ours: our messages, our anger, our loneliness, our need to be right. Guard the children who move between two houses, and give them adults who are safe and steady. Where a parent is dangerous, protect the children and the parent who protects them. You took the children in your arms and blessed them. Do it again, through us. Amen.
reflection: What have the children in my life been carrying that was never theirs to carry?
Where have I asked a child to be my messenger, my confidant, or my judge, even without meaning to?
If I am a child of divorce, what am I still carrying, and who could help me set it down?
sessions.teaching:
The adults chose the divorce, or one of them did. The children chose none of it, and they live inside all of it. They pack a bag every other Friday and learn which house has which rules and which subjects not to mention at dinner. Young children often believe the divorce happened because of something they did. Older children often believe they could fix it, or that it falls to them to keep a parent from falling apart. Grown children whose parents divorce late lose the home they went back to and the story of where they came from. None of them signed anything, and all of them live with the result.

The letter to the Ephesians was written into a world where Roman law gave a father authority over his children for as long as he lived. It says, "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4), and the parallel in the letter to the Colossians gives the reason: "so they will not become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). The command limits the one who held the power. In a divorce both parents hold that kind of power, usually while hurt and exhausted, which is when it is most easily misused.

The same passage begins with the children: "Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right" (Ephesians 6:1), and it quotes the commandment, "Honor your father and mother" (Ephesians 6:2). The commandment names both. A divorce ends a marriage, not a child's father or mother. When a parent recruits a child against the other parent, by running them down, asking the child to report back, or making the child choose, the child is asked to carry a loyalty conflict God never assigned. Honor never means submitting to abuse, and a parent who protects a child from a dangerous parent is not teaching dishonor. But where the other parent is safe, the child should be free to love them without guilt.

Those who work with children of divorce warn against the roles children get pushed into: messenger, spy, confidant, judge, the prize that proves which parent is loved more. Most parents who push a child into these roles don't set out to. They are lonely and frightened, and the child is there. Many of us can name a time it happened in our own home or a friend's, and it can't be stopped until someone notices it.

Two women once came before Solomon, each claiming the same living baby, and the king ordered the child cut in two. "Then the woman whose son was alive spoke to the king because she yearned with compassion for her son" (1 Kings 3:26), and begged him to give the baby to the other woman rather than kill him. The story shows the king's wisdom and is not a rule for custody. But it shows what love for a child looks like when adults are fighting: the true mother would rather lose her case than see the child torn apart. In ordinary co-parenting that may mean giving up a holiday that matters to you. Where the other parent is dangerous, the same love fights, through the right channels, to keep the child safe.

Children of divorce often carry guilt that isn't theirs. Ezekiel spoke to exiles who quoted a bitter proverb: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge" (Ezekiel 18:2). God refused to let them keep saying it and held each of them answerable for his own life: "A son will not bear the iniquity of his father" (Ezekiel 18:20). The prophet knew that one generation's choices shape the next; what he denied is that guilt is inherited. A child may live with the consequences of a divorce for a long time. The child does not carry the blame.

Then comes co-parenting, and here the session draws a line churches have sometimes blurred. Paul writes, "If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone" (Romans 12:18), and both qualifiers matter. With an ex who is difficult, peace is the work: brief written messages, a shared calendar, no commentary on the other home, and children free to love both parents. With an ex who hits, threatens, stalks, controls, or endangers the children, peace may not be possible, and the work is protection: a family lawyer, an advocate from the National Domestic Violence Hotline, protective orders, supervised visits where a court allows them. No church should tell such a parent to keep the peace at the children's expense. Custody law varies by state, and nothing here is legal advice.

When the disciples kept children away from Jesus, "He was indignant" (Mark 10:14), and he took the children in his arms. Children had no legal standing and nothing to offer, which is why the disciples treated them as an interruption. A church that follows him will notice the children who move between two houses and know them by their own names rather than their parents' story. Children are not the casualties of someone else's story. They are persons in it, with their own grief and their own place before God.

scriptureStudy.note: "Honor your father and mother" (Ephesians 6:2). The commandment names both parents, and a divorce ends a marriage, not a child's father or mother. A child asked to take sides is asked to carry what God never assigned.

"Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord." The letter limits the power of the one who held it, and the letter to the Colossians names what is at stake: "so they will not become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21).
"Give the living baby to the first woman. By no means should you kill him; she is his mother" (1 Kings 3:27). The woman who loved the child would rather lose her claim than see him divided.

"A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son" (Ezekiel 18:20). God refuses the exiles' proverb about sour grapes. Consequences reach the next generation; guilt does not pass down.
"God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies" (Genesis 21:17). A household split by rivalry sent a mother and her son into the wilderness, and Scripture says God heard the boy himself.

"Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!" (Mark 10:14). Jesus was indignant when his disciples turned children away. The children of divorce are not an interruption to the church's work.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long debate about what divorce does to children, and hold it honestly in both directions. Two long studies, both listed at the back, have shaped the conversation. One followed children of divorcing families in California for twenty-five years and argued that the effects often surfaced in adulthood, especially in their own attempts at lasting relationships. The other, a larger study, argued that most children of divorce grow into reasonably well-adjusted adults, and that much depends on the conflict around them and the quality of their parenting. Together they refuse two comfortable stories: that children simply bounce back, and that a child of divorce is doomed. Research can describe what children carry. It cannot tell a child that the guilt is not theirs (Ezekiel 18:20), or give a child the Father the psalm promises: "Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me" (Psalm 27:10).

Then ask what a church would do differently. Does its children's ministry know which children move between two homes? Is a child who misses every other Sunday treated as uncommitted? Are there safe, trusted adults, screened under the church's safeguarding policy, who can stand near a child whose world has split?
sessions.caseStudy:
Imagine a father in your group who shares custody of two children, nine and twelve. In the third session he says, with a laugh that isn't quite a laugh, that his daughter has become his best friend since the divorce. She asks how he is doing every night, and he tells her the truth, including what her mother did.

The room may soften toward him, and he does need care. But don't let the moment pass. Read Ephesians 6:4 and ask, gently, what a twelve-year-old does with an adult's grief and anger. Let someone name the difference between closeness and a child carrying what belongs to an adult. Afterward, speak with him privately, without shaming him. Help him find one adult who could hear what he has been telling his daughter, and encourage him to tell her she may love her mother. If anything suggests a child is unsafe in either home, follow your church's policy and the law.

Use this to show the room how easily love for a child can turn the child into a confidant, and how much freedom a child gains when an adult takes the weight back.

memoryVerse.text: Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

sessions.title: Where You Go, I Will Go
sessions.aim: To face honestly what stepfamilies live with, from loyalty binds and the stepparent's place on the outside to children grieving what a remarriage ends, and to read Ruth and Naomi as a family made by covenant loyalty rather than blood, a love offered long before it was received.
sessions.summary:
A blended family begins with a wedding, but it is born out of loss. The children lost the family they knew; the adults lost a marriage they meant to keep, or a spouse they buried; and sometimes a remarriage ends a hope a child never said aloud, that their parents might get back together. A stepparent may love a child who doesn't want their love.

The book of Ruth tells of a family held together by something other than blood. After famine and three deaths, a widow named Naomi turned home to Bethlehem and urged her two widowed daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. One went back, and Ruth clung to her: "For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16). Then the story tells the truth. When they arrived, Naomi told the town, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21), with Ruth standing beside her. Love was offered long before it was received. By the end of the book the women of Bethlehem told Naomi that Ruth loved her and was better to her than seven sons. A family made by covenant is made slowly, and mostly on ordinary days.

keyScripture.why: "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her" (Ruth 1:14), and Ruth bound herself with an oath to Naomi's people, Naomi's God, and Naomi's grave (Ruth 1:16-17). It is a family made by covenant loyalty rather than blood, and the rest of the book shows how slowly, and how honestly, such a family grows.

discussion.q: If you live in a blended family, or grew up in one, what is one ordinary collision you didn't see coming, and what was underneath it?
discussion.behind: Start concrete and a little lighter, then go underneath; the small collisions usually carry the large losses. Let people laugh if they need to, but don't let anyone mock an absent ex or a stepchild.

discussion.q: Read Ruth 1:6-18. Naomi urges both women to go home, and she blesses them. Orpah goes; Ruth clings. Is Orpah the villain of the story? What does the text actually say about her?
discussion.behind: The text doesn't condemn Orpah. Naomi urged her to go, kissed her, and prayed she would find rest in a new husband's home (Ruth 1:9); going back was the sensible choice. In a blended family some members won't draw close, and their distance is not always rejection. Ruth's clinging is a gift, not a test everyone else failed.

discussion.q: Read Ruth 1:19-22. Naomi tells the town, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21), while Ruth stands beside her. What is it like to offer love that the other person can't yet see, and what kept Ruth from leaving?
discussion.behind: This is the heart of the session for stepparents. Ruth had just sworn her life to Naomi, and Naomi spoke as if she had come home with nothing; the narrator names Ruth in the next verse (Ruth 1:22). Let stepparents say how that feels without turning it into a complaint against a child.

discussion.q: A child may feel that warming to a stepparent betrays the parent who isn't there. How can a stepparent, and the child's own parent, make it safe for a child to love everyone without choosing?
discussion.behind: Name the loyalty bind plainly. Those who counsel stepfamilies commonly advise stepparents to build a relationship before taking on discipline, to let the child's own parent lead correction at first, and never to compete with the absent parent. Telling a child in plain words that they don't have to choose can free them.

discussion.q: The women of Bethlehem eventually told Naomi that Ruth loved her and was better to her than seven sons (Ruth 4:15). The book never says how long that took. What would it mean for your family to measure trust in years rather than weeks?
discussion.behind: Close on time, and on self-implication. Adults often want a new family to work quickly, partly because a happy household would prove the new marriage was right, and pressure usually slows love down. Ask each person, starting with yourself, to name one thing they are trying to hurry.

objections.objection: A family is a family. If you love the kids like your own, they'll come around. All this talk about loyalty binds and stepparent roles just makes it complicated.
objections.response: Grant what is good in it. Love is the point, and many stepparents have loved children who are not theirs by blood with a faithfulness that puts others to shame. But love that insists on being received on its own schedule becomes pressure, and children feel pressure as one more thing they didn't choose. A child who already has a mother may not want another one, however kind, and that is not ingratitude. It is loyalty, a virtue we hope they keep. Ruth didn't demand Naomi's affection. She worked, and she stayed: "And she lived with her mother-in-law" (Ruth 2:23). In time it was Naomi who began to seek Ruth's good (Ruth 3:1). Love that waits is still love.

objections.objection: My stepchildren's mother tells them lies about me, and my husband won't stand up to her. Why should I keep being patient?
objections.response: Your frustration is real, and patience is not passivity. Some of what you describe belongs to the adults. Your husband is the children's parent, and it is fair to ask him, privately and firmly, to protect the children from being used against you and to take the lead with their mother; a counselor who understands stepfamilies can help you stand together. Patience here means refusing to answer lies with lies or to make the children carry your side of the story, and trusting that children see more over time than adults think. Paul's word fits: "Do not repay anyone evil for evil" (Romans 12:17). And if the other parent's behavior ever threatens the children's safety, that is a matter for a lawyer and an advocate, not for patience.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who in your household, or your wider family, may be offering you love that you haven't been able to receive yet, and what would it take for you to notice it?
sessions.practice: This week, choose one ordinary, pressure-free thing to do with a stepchild or a stepparent: a drive, a meal, a shared chore, a game, with no agenda and no test of affection. If you are a remarried couple, agree on one house rule, with the child's own parent enforcing it for now. If you grew up in a blended family, tell God honestly what you lost and what you were given. Read the four short chapters of Ruth. If anyone in your home is being hurt or threatened, the answer is safety, not patience: call 911 in immediate danger or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233, and if a child is being harmed, call the police or your state's child protective services. For more on stepfamilies, see /life/the-blended-family.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you settle the lonely in families, and you made a family on a road out of Moab from a widow's grief and a foreigner's loyalty. Our homes hold more than one history and more than one grief. Give the stepparents here the patience of Ruth, who kept loving before she was seen. Give the children freedom to love without choosing, and room to grieve. Give remarried couples unity and wisdom. Where we are hurrying what only time and faithfulness can grow, slow us down. You adopted us when we had no claim on you. Teach us to make room for one another. Amen.
reflection: What did each person in my household lose when this family began, and have we said those losses out loud?
Where am I offering love that hasn't been received yet, and what keeps me from leaving or from pressing?
What am I trying to hurry in my family that only time and faithfulness can grow?
sessions.teaching:
A blended family begins with a wedding, but it is born out of loss. The children lost the family they knew, through divorce or a parent's death; the adults lost a marriage they meant to keep, or a spouse they buried. For some children a remarriage ends a hope they never said aloud, that their parents might find their way back to each other, so the wedding that feels like a beginning to the adults can feel like a second ending to a child. Before a stepfamily can become a family, it has to make room for grief no one in it has finished feeling.

Then come the collisions: different rules, different ways of keeping Christmas, different wounds. A stepparent walks into a bond between parent and child that is older than the marriage and finds that, for now, they are on the outside of it. A child may like the stepparent and feel guilty for it. Those who counsel stepfamilies say plainly that becoming a family takes years, not months; they commonly advise stepparents to build a relationship before taking on discipline, to let the child's own parent lead correction at first, and never to compete with the absent parent. Christians should receive that as wisdom.

The book of Ruth gives us a family held together by something other than blood. Set in the days of the judges, three generations before David, it opens with famine and three funerals. Naomi, widowed and bereaved of both sons in Moab, set out for Bethlehem with her two Moabite daughters-in-law. On the road she urged them to go home and blessed them: "May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me" (Ruth 1:8). The word is hesed, loyal love that keeps faith beyond duty. She prayed that each would find rest in a new husband's home (Ruth 1:9). Orpah kissed her goodbye and went home, a sensible choice, and the text doesn't condemn her.

But "Ruth clung to her" (Ruth 1:14), with the same Hebrew verb Genesis uses when a man is "united to his wife" (Genesis 2:24), and she made one of the best-known vows in Scripture, often read at weddings, though she spoke it to her mother-in-law: "For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried" (Ruth 1:16-17). Her oath, calling on the LORD to punish her if she broke it, was a solemn covenant, binding her to a family that neither blood nor law required her to keep.

Then the story tells the truth. Naomi "stopped trying to persuade her" (Ruth 1:18), and no word between them on the road is recorded. When the town came out, Naomi said, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21), with Ruth standing beside her. The narrator, as if to set the record straight, names her in the next line: "So Naomi returned from the land of Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess" (Ruth 1:22). Grief can keep a person from seeing the love in front of them, and many stepparents know what it is to be treated as though they were not there.

What Ruth did next was not dramatic. She gleaned barley so they could eat, and she stayed: "And she lived with her mother-in-law" (Ruth 2:23). Naomi began to hope in the LORD, "who has not withdrawn His kindness from the living or the dead" (Ruth 2:20), and by the third chapter she was the one seeking Ruth's good: "should I not seek a resting place for you, that it may be well with you?" (Ruth 3:1). At the end the women of Bethlehem said of Ruth, "For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth" (Ruth 4:15), an extraordinary thing to say where sons were prized. The women who had heard Naomi call herself empty now named what Ruth had been to her.

Ruth's son became the grandfather of David (Ruth 4:17), and Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). The child Joseph raised in Nazareth was not his son by blood; the angel gave Joseph the naming of the boy (Matthew 1:21,25), and Luke says Jesus "was regarded as the son of Joseph" (Luke 3:23). The gospel makes family this way. God sent his Son "that we might receive our adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:5). Christians belong to God's household by adoption, which is reason enough never to treat a stepfamily as a lesser kind of family.

Scripture doesn't romanticize households built from more than one history. When Jacob loved Joseph more than his other sons, the sons of several mothers, "they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him" (Genesis 37:4). Remarried adults can favor their own children without noticing, and children notice. We are also tempted to hurry, since a happy home would prove the new marriage right. "Love is patient, love is kind" (1 Corinthians 13:4), and in a stepfamily patience is less a feeling than a decision made each morning, like Ruth walking back out to the fields. None of this asks anyone to endure abuse; where someone in the home is being hurt, safety comes first. Otherwise the work is slow, and it is meant to be.

scriptureStudy.note: "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her" (Ruth 1:14). The Hebrew verb for clinging is the one used when a man is "united to his wife" (Genesis 2:24), and Ruth's oath binds her to Naomi's people, God, and grave.
"I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:21). Naomi says it with Ruth beside her, and the narrator names Ruth in the next verse. Grief can hide love standing in plain sight.
"And she lived with her mother-in-law" (Ruth 2:23). Ruth's ordinary work brings home grain, and Naomi begins to hope. Trust grows through faithful, unremarkable days.

"For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth" (Ruth 4:15). The women of Bethlehem name what Ruth has been to Naomi. A family made by loyalty is recognized by its community.

"When Joseph's brothers saw that their father loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak a kind word to him" (Genesis 37:4). Scripture tells the truth about favoritism among the children of different mothers.
"So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God" (Galatians 4:7). The gospel makes family by adoption, not by birth.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the question of what makes a family. The ancient world built families on blood, land, and inheritance, and Israel's law worked to keep land within a family through its nearest of kin (Leviticus 25:25), which is part of what makes Ruth's story striking: a foreign widow joins a family by oath and loyalty, and the customs of redemption are put to work for her and for Naomi. Jesus went further. When his mother and brothers stood outside asking for him, after his family had set out to take custody of him (Mark 3:21,31), he said that "whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother" (Mark 3:35).

C. S. Lewis, in The Four Loves (1960), described affection as the humblest of the loves, the warmth that grows among people thrown together by circumstance rather than chosen, which can come to include people we would never have picked. That describes a stepfamily's best hope with some precision: not instant love, but affection grown from shared meals and years of ordinary days. A group might ask how a church could honor stepparents without erasing absent parents, and treat the children of more than one marriage simply as children of the church.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group married a widower two years ago. His daughter, now fourteen, is polite to her in public and cold at home. In the fourth session the stepmother says, close to tears, that she has tried everything, from the girl's favorite meals to every game on the schedule, and that last week the girl told her she will never be her mother.

The room may rush to reassure her, or someone may say the girl needs discipline. Slow it down. Read Ruth 1:19-22 and ask what Ruth heard Naomi say, and what Ruth did next. Let someone name that the girl is grieving her own mother, and that her loyalty is not a failure. Ask the stepmother, gently, what it would look like to lower the goal from winning the girl over to one ordinary, pressure-free hour together, and to let the girl's father lead on anything that feels like correction. Encourage the couple to see a counselor who understands stepfamilies.

Use this to show the room that love which waits is still love, and that a child's loyalty to a parent who died or left deserves respect.
