sessions.title: The Lonely in Families
sessions.aim: To see the church as the household through which God settles the lonely in families, to name the two ways churches fail divorced and remarried people, pretending and shaming, and to describe a welcome that tells the truth, keeps people safe, and makes room at the table.
sessions.summary:
Many people find after a divorce that the hardest door to walk through is the church's. Some congregations met them with a verdict: a quoted verse, a quiet removal from the places they served, a story passed along as a prayer request. Others met them with silence: friends who stopped calling and ministries built as though every family were intact. Remarried couples and stepfamilies can feel the same chill, wondering whether their family counts.

Psalm 68, which bears David's name, praises the God who marches in victory and then says what kind of king he is: "A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation. God settles the lonely in families" (Psalm 68:5-6). The letter of James defines pure religion in the same terms, "to care for orphans and widows in their distress" (James 1:27). Jesus called those who do the will of God his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35). When he met a woman at a well who had had five husbands, he named her history plainly and treated her with respect, and her town came to hear him because of her (John 4:16-19,39). That is the welcome this session is after: no pretending and no shaming. No one starts over from nothing, but no one has to start over alone.

keyScripture.why: "A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation. God settles the lonely in families" (Psalm 68:5-6). In a hymn to God's victory, the psalm says what kind of king he is, and the letter of James makes the same care the test of pure religion (James 1:27).

discussion.q: Think of a time you walked into a church carrying something you were ashamed of. What did people do or say that helped, and what made you want to leave?
discussion.behind: Let the room describe the verdict and the silence from the receiving end. Receive it without defending any particular church, including your own. If someone describes spiritual abuse, believe them and follow up privately. Anyone may pass. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 68:4-6 and James 1:26-27. Who are the people God is said to care for, and why might the letter of James put the bridled tongue right next to the care of widows and orphans?
discussion.behind: Widows and orphans were among the most exposed people of the ancient world. A divorced parent is not a widow, so don't flatten the text, but the distress the letter names is close kin to what a broken household leaves behind. And verse 26 calls religion with an unbridled tongue worthless, which bears on how a church talks about anyone's divorce.

discussion.q: Read John 4:16-19. Jesus names the woman's history plainly, and twice tells her she has spoken the truth. The text doesn't say why she had five husbands. What do readers often assume about her, and what does Jesus do instead?
discussion.behind: Be fair to both readings. Many have read her history as a pattern of sexual sin, an old and widely held reading. Others note that women in her world were often widowed or sent away, and that Jesus doesn't call her a sinner. Either way, he neither pretends nor shames.

discussion.q: Churches tend to fail divorced and remarried people in two ways: pretending nothing happened, or treating them as permanently less than others. Where have you seen each, and which is your church's temptation, or your own?
discussion.behind: This is the self-implication for the whole study. Ask people to name their own temptation before their church's. Remember that churches differ in good conscience on remarriage and church office, and that holding a conviction is not the same as shaming anyone.

discussion.q: Jesus said whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35). Name one concrete thing your church, or you, could do in the next month to make someone whose family has broken feel like family.
discussion.behind: Make it specific: a seat at a holiday table, childcare during a court date, a standing lunch, an adult who will sit with a child whose parent is absent, a calendar that doesn't assume two parents in one house. Write the ideas down and give them to a pastor. Leave the study with a direction rather than a resolution.

objections.objection: If the church makes divorced and remarried people too comfortable, it will look as if we approve of divorce. Some distance is a form of faithfulness.
objections.response: Grant what is right in it. A church that never speaks about the lifelong vow will teach its children that marriage is disposable, and churches differ in good conscience about remarriage and church office. Teaching what you believe is not shaming anyone. But distance is a strange way to teach. Jesus asked the woman at the well for a drink, spoke plainly about her five husbands, and then accepted her neighbors' invitation and stayed in her town two days (John 4:40). A church can hold its convictions and still be the place where a divorced person is fed, prayed for, and known by name. Convictions about marriage are more likely to be heard from people who kept a chair at the table.

objections.objection: I've been hurt by the church over my divorce. Why should I trust it to be my family now?
objections.response: You may have every reason not to, and the church's failure is the church's to confess, not yours to explain. Verdicts, gossip, and a silence that felt like a door closing all did real harm. This session doesn't ask you to go back to a church that hurt you. It asks whether you would let one or two people be family to you in small ways, a meal, a ride, a seat at a table, and see whether they keep their word. Trust is rebuilt slowly, and it should be. If you were spiritually abused, the care page at /help/church-hurt is a place to start. The God of Psalm 68 settles the lonely in families, sometimes one person at a time.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who in your church, or your life, has been missing from a family table since their marriage ended, and what is one way you could make room for them?
sessions.practice: This week, do one concrete thing to make room for someone whose family has broken: invite them to a meal, watch their children during a court date or a hard appointment, sit with them in church, or ask them to join you for the next holiday. If you are the one who has been alone, accept one invitation, or ask one person for one specific kind of help. Pray Psalm 68:5-6 each day. If you are in danger at home, call 911 in an emergency, or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of the fatherless and the widow, you settle the lonely in families, and you have made us your household by adoption. We confess that your church has sometimes closed its doors with a verdict and sometimes with silence, and that we have done both. Forgive us. Make us a family where the divorced are known by name and not by their story, where children between two houses are safe and seen, and where no one in danger is sent back to it. We have not started over from nothing. We start again from where you found us, and we are not alone. Amen.
reflection: Where have I, or my church, pretended, and where have we shamed?
Who has been family to me when my own family broke, and to whom could I be family now?
What would it take for my church to be a place where a divorced person, a remarried couple, and a child between two houses all know they belong?
sessions.teaching:
Many people find after a divorce that the hardest door to walk through is the church's. Some congregations met them with a verdict: a verse quoted in the lobby, a quiet word that they should step back from where they served, a story passed along as a prayer request. Others met them with silence. The verdict and the silence look like opposites, but they leave a person in the same place, outside.

Psalm 68 bears David's name and is among the hardest texts in the Psalter, a processional hymn of God's march from Sinai to Zion. In the middle of all that thunder it says what kind of king this is: "A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation. God settles the lonely in families" (Psalm 68:5-6). The psalm sees no conflict between his holiness and his care for the people a household has failed, and his answer to loneliness is a family.

The letter of James makes that care the test of real religion: "Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world" (James 1:27). Orphans and widows were among the most exposed people in the ancient world, without a man to provide legal protection or income. A divorced mother is not a widow, and a child with two living parents is not an orphan. But the distress the letter names is close kin to what a household's breaking leaves behind: one income where there were two, a man eating Thanksgiving dinner by himself. And the verse before warns that whoever "does not bridle his tongue" has a worthless religion (James 1:26). Gossip about someone's divorce, even dressed as a prayer request, is that unbridled tongue.

Jesus knew family strain from the inside; his family set out to take custody of him, saying, "He is out of His mind" (Mark 3:21), and "even His own brothers did not believe in Him" (John 7:5). When his mother and brothers stood outside asking for him, he looked at those around him and said, "For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother" (Mark 3:35). He promised a hundredfold of family "in the present age" (Mark 10:30) to those who left home for his sake. That promise has an address, and it is the church. From the cross, a dying son provided for his mother and made a household of two grieving people: "So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home" (John 19:27).

At a well in Samaria, Jesus asked a woman to call her husband, and when she said she had none, he answered, "You are correct to say that you have no husband. In fact, you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband. You have spoken truthfully" (John 4:17-18). Many readers have taken her history as a pattern of sexual sin, an old and widely held reading. Others note that the text never says why she had five husbands, that women in her world were often widowed or sent away by husbands, and that Jesus doesn't call her a sinner or tell her to repent. Either way, he names her history without pretending and treats her as someone worth talking to, without contempt. And "Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Jesus because of the woman's testimony" (John 4:39).

What would it look like for a church to settle the lonely in families after a divorce? It begins with refusing to assume: "The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him" (Proverbs 18:17), and a congregation that has heard one side of a divorce should be slow to speak and quick to stay. That proverb is never a reason to doubt someone who says they are afraid; a church believes that person and helps them get safe. Then comes help that outlasts the first month, when the calls tend to stop: meals, rides, childcare during a court date, a chair at the table on the first holidays alone. Children's ministries can learn which children move between two homes, and leaders can learn the signs of abuse and the law on reporting, so that no frightened spouse is sent home. A church can teach what it believes about remarriage and church office without making anyone a second-class Christian.

None of us leads this from outside. Many of us who belong to churches have done one or the other, quoting a verse we hadn't read in its setting or avoiding a friend in the parking lot because we didn't know what to say. What will change that is people who stay. Taking marriage seriously and taking seriously the people whose marriages have ended were never opposites; Jesus did both in one conversation at a well.

This study has been about starting over, and it should end honestly. No one starts over from nothing. The history comes along, and so do the children, the former spouse, the grief, and sometimes the guilt. What Scripture offers is a God who was present for all of it, who hates the breaking of faith and is near to everyone it broke, and who settles the lonely in families. The church is meant to be one of those families. Whether it will be, in this town and this congregation, depends in part on the people in this room.

"Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress" (James 1:27). The verse before it warns against an unbridled tongue. Real religion cares for the exposed and refuses to gossip about them.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the early church's sense of itself as a family. The New Testament calls believers brothers and sisters again and again and speaks of the church as a household (Galatians 6:10; Ephesians 2:19), and the first believers kept a daily distribution of food for widows (Acts 6:1). Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing Life Together in 1938 after the Gestapo had closed his underground seminary, warned that whoever loves a dream of community more than the community itself will destroy it, and that Christian community is a gift God gives rather than an ideal we build. A church that dreams of being a church of intact families is loving a dream. The real church is made of the people God has actually given it.

Weigh, too, a question faithful churches answer differently. The letters to Timothy and Titus ask that an overseer or elder be "the husband of but one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6). Some churches read the phrase as excluding a man who has divorced and remarried, and some any man who has divorced, because the office is meant to show a congregation what a kept vow looks like. Others read it as describing a faithful, one-woman man, judged by his present life rather than his history, because the grace that restores a sinner can restore him to service. Others read it as forbidding a man to have more than one wife at a time. A group can state each view fairly and ask how a church holding any of them can keep divorced people at the center of its life.
sessions.caseStudy:
Imagine that in the final session a woman who was divorced several years ago says she has stopped coming to the church's family events. The flyers always show a mother, a father, and children, and the Christmas dinner is organized by couples. No one has ever said anything unkind to her; she just doesn't feel there is a place for her. A deacon in the group answers, a little defensively, that the church can't stop teaching about marriage because some people are divorced.

Don't let this become a debate between the two of them. Thank them both, and read Psalm 68:5-6 and James 1:27. Ask the group what it would look like to keep teaching about marriage and also make room at the table. Someone may suggest a holiday meal for households of every shape, or asking the woman to help plan it if she would like to. Write the ideas down for the pastor.

Use this to show the room that pretending can wound as surely as shaming, and that a church's convictions about marriage and its welcome to the divorced don't have to compete.

memoryVerse.text: Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

leaderPrimer:
Your room may hold all of these at once: someone whose spouse moved out last month, someone divorced twenty years ago who still feels like a second-class Christian, someone who left and isn't sure they were right to, a remarried couple, a worn-out stepparent, a grown child of divorce, and someone afraid of the person they married. Most have already heard either a verdict or a silence from a church. The hazard of leading this study is the urge to rule on someone's divorce: who was at fault, whether they had grounds, whether they may remarry. Don't. You will hear one side of every story (Proverbs 18:17), and the group is not a court. That proverb guards against verdicts on people who aren't in the room; it is never a reason to doubt someone who tells you they are afraid.

Safety comes before every other conversation, including reconciliation. If anyone says or hints that they are afraid of a spouse or former spouse, or that the children are not safe, act on it. Never counsel anyone to stay in danger or to return to it, never urge anyone to confront an abusive person, and never suggest that a frightened couple talk it out together; joint counseling with someone who has been abusive isn't recommended, and mediation may not be safe either. Leaving can be the most dangerous time, which is why a safety plan matters: point them to the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788, and to 911 in immediate danger. Ask how it is safe to contact them, since phones may be watched. Don't place a separated couple in the same group, and where there has been abuse, don't consider it at all.

If anyone speaks of not wanting to live, of suicide, or of everyone being better off without them, take it seriously every time. Asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide does not put the idea in their head. Don't move on to the next question. Speak with them privately, stay with them, and call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, together; in immediate danger, call 911. If a child is being harmed or is at risk, the child's safety comes first; call the police or your state's child protective services. Church leaders may be mandated reporters, and the laws vary by state; know your obligations before the study begins. Never ask anyone to disclose abuse, danger, or thoughts of suicide in the group. When it comes out anyway, stop, thank them, talk privately as soon as you can, and connect them to help.

Set the rule of confidentiality at the first meeting and state its limits just as plainly: no one's story leaves the room, not even as a prayer request, but if someone is in danger or a child is being harmed, you will not keep that secret, and you may be required to report it. If a teenager comes with a parent, let them pass on any question, never ask them to describe either home, and follow your church's safeguarding policy for any conversation afterward. You are not a lawyer or a counselor, and nothing in this guide is legal advice. Divorce and custody law vary by state; send people to a family law attorney, or to legal aid if money is tight, before they sign anything, and to a licensed counselor for grief, a struggling child, or a stepfamily under strain (/help/refer-to-counselor explains how to find one). The care page at /help/divorce gathers first steps, and the eight-week plan at /plans/divorce can carry someone between sessions.

Some questions this study raises are open among faithful Christians, and the guide leaves them open. The largest is remarriage after divorce. One view holds that marriage binds until death, so that remarriage while a former spouse lives is not permitted. It rests on Mark 10:11-12, Luke 16:18, and 1 Corinthians 7:39; it was largely the view of the early church and, in its own form, is the teaching of the Catholic Church; and its comfort is a vow kept the way God keeps his, with the door to reconciliation left open. A second view holds that sexual unfaithfulness and desertion free the wronged spouse to divorce and remarry. It rests on Jesus' exception in Matthew 19:9 and Paul's "not bound in such cases" (1 Corinthians 7:15); many Protestant churches have held it since the Reformation, and the Westminster Confession teaches it; and its comfort is that the betrayed and abandoned are not made to carry the betrayer's sin for life. A third, wider view counts abuse and other grave breaking of the vows as desertion or covenant-breaking. It points to 1 Corinthians 7:15, to the law's protection of a neglected wife in Exodus 21:10-11, and to Malachi's anger at violence done to a wife; many Protestant churches now hold some form of it; and its comfort is that no one is bound to a covenant the other turned into danger. The Orthodox churches, by a pastoral mercy called economia, allow a second marriage with prayers of repentance. A related open question is whether divorce or remarriage bears on church office. Some churches read "the husband of but one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2) as excluding a man who has divorced and remarried, and some any man who has divorced, guarding the example the office sets; others read it as describing a faithful, one-woman man, judged by his present life rather than his history, guarding the grace that restores; others read it as forbidding a man to have more than one wife at a time. These questions divide churches, not the faith. James Bell's own landing is not given in this guide, and your church's pastors and tradition will have more to say. Let people disagree and remain brothers and sisters. What is not open is the floor, and every one of these views can stand on it: Scripture never requires anyone to stay in danger; abuse is a breaking of the marriage covenant by the abuser, not by the spouse who flees, whatever a church then holds about remarriage; and no divorce is beyond God's forgiveness for anyone who confesses.

You don't need to be divorced to lead this study, or to have a perfect marriage. If you have been divorced, ask a co-leader to share the room, keep your own support outside the group, and never make your story the template for anyone else's. If you haven't, don't lead from above; most of us have broken faith in smaller ways. Expect grief around holidays and anniversaries. Five sessions will not end anyone's grief. They can end the hiding, and some of the loneliness.

faq.a: The line comes from Malachi 2:16, spoken to men who had broken faith with the wives of their youth (Malachi 2:13-14). The Hebrew is difficult, and translations differ. The Berean Standard Bible, like the King James, makes God the one who hates divorce: "For I hate divorce" (Malachi 2:16). The NIV of 2011 and the CSB read it as describing the husband who hates his wife and divorces her, and the ESV reads it in much the same way. On any of these readings the anger falls on the one who breaks faith, and the passage stands with the wife who was sent away. Nothing in it says God hates the people a divorce has wounded, or that he is finished with anyone who comes to him.

faq.q: Is divorce a sin? Am I living in sin because I'm divorced?
faq.a: Scripture treats the breaking of a marriage as a real wrong (Matthew 19:8). But being divorced and having sinned are not the same thing. Paul tells the believer whose unbelieving spouse walks out to "let him go" (1 Corinthians 7:15); the one who was left didn't do the leaving, and no one sins by getting themselves and their children away from danger. Faithful Christians differ on which grounds make a divorce right, as the second session explains. Where you did wrong, you can name it and be forgiven (1 John 1:9). Divorce is not the unforgivable sin, and it is not your name.

Faithful churches answer this differently, and the question divides churches, not the faith. One view holds that marriage binds until death: "A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives" (1 Corinthians 7:39), and Mark and Luke record Jesus' saying without an exception (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18). The Catholic Church teaches that a valid, consummated marriage between baptized Christians cannot be dissolved, though its tribunals can declare that a marriage was never valid. This view keeps a vow as God keeps his. A second view holds that adultery or desertion frees the wronged spouse to remarry, reading Jesus' exception (Matthew 19:9) and Paul's "not bound in such cases" (1 Corinthians 7:15); it won't make the betrayed carry the betrayer's sin for life. A third view counts abuse and other grave breaking of the vows as desertion too, since "God has called you to live in peace" (1 Corinthians 7:15). The Orthodox churches, by economia, allow a second marriage with prayers of repentance. Take your question to a pastor who will hear your whole story.

faq.q: My spouse hurts or frightens me. Does the Bible say I have to stay?
faq.a: No. Scripture never requires anyone to stay in danger, and no church should send you home to it. Hitting, threats, stalking, and control are abuse, and abuse is a breaking of the marriage covenant by the one who does it, not by the one who flees. Even Christians who hold the strictest view of remarriage teach that separation can be right, and Paul's instructions already make room for a spouse who has separated (1 Corinthians 7:11). In immediate danger, call 911. The National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788, can help you plan, including for leaving, which can be the most dangerous time. Use a phone or computer your spouse can't reach, and tell your lawyer about the abuse early.

faq.q: My spouse left me. Was it my fault?
faq.a: You can own what was yours without owning what was theirs. If you were cold, harsh, or unfaithful, confess it to God and, where it is safe and wise, to the person you hurt. But the decision to leave was theirs. When Paul wrote about a believer whose spouse walked out, he told the one who stayed to let the other go, and he laid no blame on them (1 Corinthians 7:15). If the leaving came with an affair, an addiction, or abuse, you did not cause it by failing to be enough. A counselor or a wise pastor can help you sort out what was yours.

faq.q: I was the one who left. Is there a place for me in this study?
faq.a: Yes. Some people left because staying wasn't safe, and they have nothing to repent of in leaving. Some left after a spouse's unfaithfulness. Others left for reasons they now regret. Whatever your story, you belong in the room. Where you did wrong, name it plainly to God, make what amends are possible and safe, and receive the forgiveness Scripture promises (1 John 1:9). Psalm 51, whose heading sets it after David's adultery with Bathsheba, is the prayer of a man who did grave wrong and asked to be washed clean. The God of Psalm 34 is near to the contrite as well as to the brokenhearted.

faq.q: How do I talk to my children about the divorce?
faq.a: Tell them together if that is safe, in words that fit their age, and keep it simple: the divorce is a decision the adults made, it isn't their fault, it isn't theirs to fix, and they will be loved and cared for. Don't give them the adult reasons or criticize their other parent where they can hear. Keep their routines steady, and let them be sad or angry without having to protect you. If the other parent is not safe, take the details to your lawyer and an advocate, not to the children, and tell the children, as plainly as their age allows, that keeping them safe is your job. A pediatrician or school counselor is a good first call if a child is struggling.

faq.q: I'm a stepparent, and my stepchild rejects me. What does this study say to me?
faq.a: That what you are living through is common in stepfamilies, and it doesn't by itself mean you are failing. A child who already has a mother or father may not want another one, however kind you are, and that loyalty is a virtue, not an insult. Those who counsel stepfamilies commonly advise building a relationship before taking on discipline and measuring trust in years rather than months. The fourth session reads Ruth, who heard Naomi tell the town she had come home empty (Ruth 1:21) and stayed anyway. Look after your marriage, find a counselor who understands stepfamilies, and see /life/the-blended-family for more. If anyone in the home is being hurt, safety comes before patience.

faq.q: My parents divorced when I was already an adult. Do I belong in this study?
faq.a: Yes. Grown children lose real things when their parents divorce: the home they went back to, the holidays they assumed, the story of where they came from. You're allowed to grieve. You don't have to take sides, carry messages, or become either parent's confidant; you can love them both and still tell one of them that you can't be the one they talk to about the other. The third session is partly for you. Ezekiel's word holds at any age: the consequences of your parents' choices reach you, but their guilt does not (Ezekiel 18:20).

faq.q: I'm a teenager, and my parents are divorced or remarried. Is this study for me?
faq.a: Yes. You didn't choose the divorce, and it isn't your fault or yours to fix. You don't have to carry messages between your parents, report on the other house, or take a side, and you can come to care about a stepparent without betraying the parent who isn't there. In the group you never have to share anything, and you can pass on any question. If you're ever afraid at home, or someone is hurting you, tell a school counselor, a teacher, or another adult you trust, and call 911 in an emergency. If you've had thoughts of not wanting to live, call or text 988. The third and fourth sessions are partly about you.

faq.q: Can someone who is divorced serve or lead in the church?
faq.a: Churches answer this differently, and it is another question that divides churches, not the faith. The disagreement usually concerns offices such as pastor, elder, or deacon, for which 1 Timothy and Titus ask for a man who is "the husband of but one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2,12; Titus 1:6). Some churches read the phrase as excluding a man who has divorced and remarried, and some any man who has divorced; others read it as describing a faithful, one-woman man, judged by his present life rather than his history; others read it as forbidding a man to have more than one wife at a time. Whatever your church holds, a divorced member should hear it plainly and kindly, not discover it through a quiet removal.

faq.q: I'm not a Christian, and my divorce was hard enough without a church telling me what I did wrong. Why would I come to this?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and churches have earned it. Some have treated divorced people as the guilty party and others have ignored them, and this study names both failures as the church's own. It won't hand you a verdict on your marriage, or pretend divorce is nothing. It reads the Bible's hardest words about divorce in their setting, where their anger falls on the one who broke faith and their tenderness on the one who was sent away. You don't have to believe it to find it honest. It asks only that you weigh it, and let a few people treat you like family while you do.

timeline.event: The setting of the book of Ruth, in the days when the judges ruled. A Moabite widow binds herself by oath to her mother-in-law, Naomi (Ruth 1:16-17), and Ruth's son becomes the grandfather of David (Ruth 4:17).
Malachi preaches to Judah in the Persian period, after the exile, rebuking men who have broken faith with the wives of their youth and whose offerings God no longer accepts (Malachi 2:13-16).

In Perea, east of the Jordan, Pharisees ask Jesus whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason. He answers from creation and calls Moses' certificate a concession to hardness of heart (Matthew 19:1-9).
Writing from Ephesus, Paul passes on the Lord's command to the married and takes up the case of a believer whose unbelieving spouse leaves (1 Corinthians 7:10-16).
The Mishnah is compiled. Its tractate on divorce (Gittin 9:10) records the dispute between the schools of Shammai and Hillel over the grounds on which a man may divorce his wife.

At its twenty-fourth session, the Council of Trent teaches that marriage is a sacrament and that the bond of a marriage is not dissolved by adultery, so that neither spouse may remarry while the other lives.

The Westminster Assembly completes its Confession of Faith, whose chapter on marriage and divorce allows the innocent party to divorce and remarry after adultery, and counts willful desertion that neither church nor civil magistrate can remedy as the only other sufficient cause.

California passes the Family Law Act, usually counted as the first no-fault divorce law in the United States. Taking effect in 1970, it allows a marriage to be dissolved for irreconcilable differences.
New York becomes the last state to adopt a form of no-fault divorce.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for coming. For some of you it took courage to walk into a church room to talk about divorce, and you are welcome here, whatever your story. Before we start, a few things. First, what is said here stays here, with one exception: if someone is in danger of harming themselves or someone else, or a child is being harmed, I will not keep that secret, and I may be required to get help. Second, no one has to share anything, and no one will ask you to explain your divorce or anyone else's. Third, this group is not a court, and we won't be deciding who was at fault in anyone's marriage. Fourth, if you are afraid of your spouse or former spouse, your safety comes before anything we talk about here; please talk with me afterward, or call the National Domestic Violence Hotline, whose number is on your handout. None of us stands above this subject. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and we'll sit with it a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, to the places this is actually lived: the Friday handoff, the holiday table with an empty chair, the Sunday morning you almost didn't come.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though nothing is finished, because a divorce isn't healed in an evening, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. If something tonight told you that you need help, a counselor, a lawyer, or someone to talk to, hear that as God's kindness, not failure, and talk with me afterward if you'd like help finding it. If you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988; if you are afraid of someone at home, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline on your handout; in an emergency, call 911. Then, if you can, tell me. Try the practice this week. And remember that what was said here stays here. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules on confidentiality and its limits, and say plainly that safety comes first, that the group is not a court, and that the study is not legal advice or counseling.
Week 2: Session 1, Near to the Brokenhearted, with extended time on Malachi 2:13-16 in its setting.
Week 3: Session 2, What God Has Joined, part one: Matthew 19, Mark 10, and 1 Corinthians 7 side by side.
Week 4: Session 2, part two: the three views of remarriage stated in their strongest forms, and the floor of safety beneath them.
Week 5: Session 3, Caught in the Middle, including the difference between a difficult ex and an unsafe one.
Week 6: Session 4, Where You Go, I Will Go, with the whole book of Ruth read aloud.
Week 7: Session 5, The Lonely in Families, with ideas written down for the pastors.

Week 8: Integration. Revisit the practices and memory verses, and help every person leave with one person to call, one table where they are welcome, and, if needed, a next step toward a counselor, a lawyer, or an advocate.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Near to the Brokenhearted, with the ground rules and the safety guidance set at the start.

Week 3: Sessions 3 and 4 together: the children caught in the middle and the long work of a blended family.
Week 4: Session 5, The Lonely in Families, closing with each person naming one person to call and one table where they are welcome.

bibliography.title: Divorce and Remarriage: Four Christian Views
bibliography.author: H. Wayne House, editor
bibliography.note: Published in 1990, it sets four positions side by side, each argued by a defender and answered by the others: no divorce and no remarriage, divorce but no remarriage, divorce and remarriage for adultery or desertion, and divorce and remarriage under a variety of circumstances.

bibliography.title: Remarriage after Divorce in Today's Church: 3 Views
bibliography.author: Mark L. Strauss, editor, with William A. Heth, Craig S. Keener, and Gordon J. Wenham
bibliography.note: Published in 2006, it sets three views of remarriage after divorce side by side, each argued by one of its contributors and answered by the others.

bibliography.title: Jesus and Divorce
bibliography.author: William A. Heth and Gordon J. Wenham
bibliography.note: First published in 1984, it argues that the early church largely held that a divorced believer should not remarry while a former spouse lives, and that this is the best reading of Jesus' teaching, the exception in Matthew included.

bibliography.title: Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible: The Social and Literary Context
bibliography.author: David Instone-Brewer
bibliography.note: Published in 2002, it reads Jesus against first-century Jewish divorce law and argues that the phrase any reason in Matthew 19:3 names the easy divorce Jesus rejected, while other grounds the law recognized, such as the neglect addressed in Exodus 21:10-11, were left standing; the author counts abuse among them.

bibliography.title: The Unexpected Legacy of Divorce
bibliography.author: Judith S. Wallerstein, Julia M. Lewis, and Sandra Blakeslee
bibliography.note: Published in 2000, it follows children of divorcing families in California into adulthood and argues that the effects of divorce often surfaced years later, especially in their own attempts at lasting relationships. Session 3.

bibliography.title: For Better or For Worse: Divorce Reconsidered
bibliography.author: E. Mavis Hetherington and John Kelly
bibliography.note: Published in 2002 and drawn from a large long-term study of divorced and remarried families, it argues that most children of divorce become reasonably well-adjusted adults, and that much depends on the conflict around them and the quality of their parenting. Session 3.

bibliography.title: Becoming a Stepfamily: Patterns of Development in Remarried Families
bibliography.author: Patricia L. Papernow
bibliography.note: Published in 1993, a clinician's account of the stages through which stepfamilies typically move over a period of years, and of the stepparent's early place as an outsider to the bond between parent and child. Not a Christian book.

bibliography.title: The Four Loves
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Published in 1960, it distinguishes affection, friendship, romantic love, and charity. Lewis describes affection as the humblest of the loves, growing from familiarity among people who did not choose one another, and warns that every natural love needs charity to keep it from going bad. Session 4.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Written in 1938 out of the shared life of the underground seminary the Gestapo had closed, and published in 1939. It treats Christian community as a gift of God rather than an ideal we build, and warns that a dream of community loved more than the real one destroys it. Session 5.

bibliography.title: When the Church Was a Family
bibliography.author: Joseph H. Hellerman
bibliography.note: Published in 2009, it argues that the early church understood itself as a family of brothers and sisters in the strong sense of the ancient Mediterranean world, where loyalty to one's siblings came first. Session 5.

furtherReading: Remarriage after Divorce in Today's Church: 3 Views, edited by Mark L. Strauss, for readers who want to hear three views of remarriage argued by their own defenders and answered by one another.
Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible, David Instone-Brewer, for readers who want the first-century Jewish background to Jesus' words on divorce.
Becoming a Stepfamily, Patricia L. Papernow, for remarried couples who need to know that the long, uneven road to becoming a family is normal.
The Four Loves, C. S. Lewis, for stepparents and stepchildren learning that affection grows slowly from shared ordinary life and cannot be demanded.
Life Together, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for churches that want to receive the people God has actually given them rather than the church they dreamed of.

glossary.definition: A binding relationship sealed by a promise before God. Malachi calls a wife her husband's companion "and your wife by covenant" (Malachi 2:14), with the LORD as witness, and Scripture uses the same language for God's bond with his people.
The written document Deuteronomy 24:1-4 required a husband to give a wife he sent away. It proved she was free to marry again, a protection for her, since only the husband could end the marriage.

The words "except for sexual immorality" in Matthew 19:9 and 5:32, absent from Mark and Luke. Christians read it as permitting divorce and remarriage after adultery, as permitting separation only, or as referring to betrothal or to marriages the law forbade.

Abandonment of a marriage by one spouse. Paul says that if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer "is not bound in such cases" (1 Corinthians 7:15), which Christians read either as freedom to remarry or as freedom from the duty to hold the marriage together.

Living apart without ending the marriage. Paul's instructions make room for a spouse who has separated (1 Corinthians 7:11), and even the strictest view of remarriage allows separation, including for safety.

Often called an annulment. In the Catholic Church, a tribunal's finding that what appeared to be a marriage was never a valid one. The Church teaches that a valid, consummated marriage between baptized Christians cannot be dissolved.
In the Orthodox churches, a pastoral mercy that relaxes the strict application of a rule for a person's good, by which a second marriage may be allowed, with prayers of repentance.

Divorce that does not require either spouse to prove the other guilty of wrongdoing. California's 1969 law is usually counted as the first in the United States; every state now offers some form of it.
A question that divides faithful churches but not the faith itself, such as remarriage after divorce. The creeds don't settle it, and Christians who differ on it remain brothers and sisters.
A court order that restricts an abusive person's contact with someone they have harmed. It should never replace a safety plan, and an advocate can help a person learn the options where they live.
A personal plan for staying as safe as possible while living with, leaving, or co-parenting with an abusive person. Hotline advocates help people make one.
A person required by law to report suspected child abuse or neglect. Many states include clergy, and the rules vary by state.
The pull a child feels when loving one parent, or a stepparent, seems to betray another. Adults ease it by telling children plainly that they don't have to choose.
The Berean Standard Bible's rendering of hesed in Naomi's blessing (Ruth 1:8): loyal love that keeps faith within a relationship and goes beyond duty. It is one of the key words of the book of Ruth.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Churches have tended to meet divorce in one of two ways, with a verdict or with silence, and both leave people grieving alone. This five-session study reads the Bible's hardest words about divorce in their setting, sets out the main Christian views on remarriage fairly, and turns to the children caught in the middle, the long, slow work of stepfamilies, and the church as family for people whose families have broken. It is for people walking through divorce, remarried couples, stepfamilies, and anyone who loves them. It puts safety first. Built so any volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Come as you are, history and all.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a study called Starting Over, on divorce and blended families, and before anyone braces, hear this. It won't put anyone's divorce on trial, and it won't pretend divorce doesn't matter. It's for anyone whose marriage has ended or is ending, for remarried couples and stepfamilies, and for anyone who loves them. We'll read what Jesus and Paul actually said, take the children seriously, and ask what it would mean for this church to be family to people whose families have broken. If you are afraid of someone at home, your safety comes first, and you can talk with me privately. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted" (Psalm 34:18). A five-session study for people walking through divorce, remarried couples, stepfamilies, and the churches that love them. No verdicts, no pretending, and safety first. Come as you are.
quoteCards: A divorce is a death in which no one dies.
Read in its setting, Malachi's anger falls on the one who broke faith. The verse stands with the one who was sent away.
God is near to the brokenhearted and to the contrite. In many divorces they are the same person.
Faithful churches differ on remarriage. They do not differ on this: no one is required to stay in danger.
The consequences of a divorce reach the children. The guilt does not.
Children are not messengers, spies, or judges. They are children.
A family made by covenant is made slowly, and mostly on ordinary days.
No one starts over from nothing. But no one has to start over alone.
